When a honeybee forager finds a rich source of food, she returns to the hive and performs a series of movements on the vertical surface of the comb. In the most informative of these, the waggle dance, she makes a short straight run while shaking her abdomen from side to side, then circles back to her starting point and repeats the run. The Austrian zoologist Karl von Frisch, who shared a Nobel Prize in 1973 partly for this work, argued that the dance encodes the location of the food.

According to von Frisch, the angle of the straight run relative to vertical corresponds to the angle between the food and the sun as seen from the hive. A run straight up the comb indicates food in the direction of the sun; a run tilted 40 degrees to the right of vertical indicates food 40 degrees to the right of the sun. The duration of each run, meanwhile, increases with distance, so a longer waggle signals a more distant source.

In the 1960s, some researchers challenged this account, arguing that recruited bees might find food mainly by smell, using odors carried back on the dancer's body. Later experiments helped settle the dispute. In one, published in 2005, recruits were fitted with tiny transponders and tracked by radar, and most flew in roughly the direction their dance had indicated. Odor still matters, however, particularly as recruits draw near the food.

Most known asteroids orbit the Sun in a broad belt between Mars and Jupiter. In the 1860s, the American astronomer Daniel Kirkwood noticed that they are not spread evenly across this belt. When the known asteroids were sorted by their average distance from the Sun, certain distances were almost empty. These Kirkwood gaps, as they came to be called, do not appear as empty lanes in a photograph of the sky, because asteroids on stretched, oval orbits pass through the gap distances on their way around the Sun. The gaps show up only when asteroids are counted by the average size of their orbits.

Kirkwood also proposed the explanation that astronomers still broadly accept. The gaps lie where an asteroid's orbital period would be a simple fraction of Jupiter's period of nearly twelve years. An asteroid in one of the most prominent gaps, for example, would circle the Sun three times for every orbit of Jupiter. Such an asteroid meets the giant planet at the same points in its orbit again and again, so Jupiter's small gravitational pulls add up instead of averaging out. The asteroid's orbit gradually grows more elongated until it crosses the path of Mars or Earth, and a close encounter may remove it from the belt.

Such resonances do not always clear a region, however. At certain other ratios, the repeated pulls help keep orbits stable, and asteroids gather there. One such group, the Hildas, orbits the Sun three times for every two orbits of Jupiter.

Before the early nineteenth century, a physician who wished to listen to a patient's heart or lungs usually pressed an ear directly against the chest. This method, later called immediate auscultation, had clear drawbacks. It was awkward and often embarrassing for both parties, and it was of limited use when a patient's chest was heavily padded with fat.

In 1816, according to his own later account, the French physician René Laennec was examining a young woman with symptoms of heart disease at a Paris hospital and hesitated to place his ear on her chest. Recalling that sound travels well through solid materials, he rolled several sheets of paper into a tight cylinder, placed one end over her heart, and put his ear to the other. He reported that he could hear the heartbeat more clearly than he ever had by the direct method. He soon replaced the paper with a hollow wooden tube, the first stethoscope.

The instrument itself was simple; what made Laennec's work important was the method he built around it. Over the next few years he listened to many patients, recorded the sounds he heard, and, when patients died, compared his notes with what autopsies revealed inside their chests. In this way he linked particular sounds to particular diseases of the heart and lungs, publishing his findings in 1819. His approach helped shift the physical examination toward detecting hidden internal damage rather than simply recording outward symptoms.

Sociologists had long treated close relationships, such as those with family members and good friends, as the bonds that matter most in a person's life. Granovetter argued that for some purposes, looser connections can matter more.

His evidence came partly from surveys and interviews with people in professional, technical, and managerial jobs in a suburb of Boston who had recently changed jobs. Among those who had learned of their new position through a personal contact, more had heard of it from someone they saw only occasionally or rarely than from someone they saw often. Granovetter's explanation was structural. For centuries, farming villages in much of northern Europe left part of their arable land fallow, or unplanted, each year. Under the common three-field system, one field might grow wheat, a second barley or oats, and the third would rest, so that the soil could recover its fertility and weeds could be controlled by plowing. In any given year, a third of the land therefore produced no crop at all.

During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, farmers in parts of England, especially Norfolk, increasingly replaced the fallow with fodder crops. In the best-known version, the Norfolk four-course rotation, a field grew wheat, then turnips, then barley, and then clover before the cycle began again. Turnips could be hoed while growing, which helped control weeds, and they fed livestock through the winter, when animal feed had traditionally been scarce. Clover provided hay and grazing and, though no one at the time understood why, it left the soil richer for the wheat that followed. Scientists later showed that bacteria in clover's roots convert nitrogen from the air into a form plants can use. More animals, in turn, meant more manure for the fields.

The rotation is often credited to Charles Townshend, a politician nicknamed "Turnip" Townshend for his enthusiasm for the crop. Historians now regard this as an exaggeration. The Venus flytrap grows wild only in a small coastal region of North and South Carolina, in boggy soils so poor in nitrogen that most plants struggle there. It makes up the shortfall by catching insects and spiders. Each trap consists of two lobes hinged along a midrib, and on the inner surface of each lobe stand a few stiff trigger hairs, usually three.

During the Norwegian explorer Fridtjof Nansen's voyage through the Arctic aboard the Fram in the 1890s, he noticed something puzzling: the sea ice did not drift in the direction the wind was blowing but moved off at an angle, consistently to the right of it. Nansen suspected that Earth's rotation was responsible. The problem was passed to a young Swedish physicist, Vagn Walfrid Ekman, who published a mathematical explanation in 1905.

Ekman's account rests on the Coriolis effect, the apparent deflection of moving objects caused by Earth's rotation, which in the Northern Hemisphere turns currents to the right. Wind drags the thin surface layer of the sea, and that layer, deflected, moves at an angle to the wind. It in turn drags the layer below, which is deflected further and moves more slowly, and so on downward, so that the direction of flow rotates with depth while its speed fades. Drawn as arrows, the pattern forms a spiral. When the movement of the whole wind-driven layer is added up, the net transport of water is, in theory, at right angles to the wind. Measured angles in the real ocean are often smaller, but the principle has held.

The consequences can be large. Along the coast of California, for example, winds blowing toward the equator in spring and summer push surface water away from the shore. Colder water rises from below to replace it, bringing up nutrients that support abundant marine life.

In the late seventeenth century, London's coffeehouses served as informal offices for the city's merchants. Each attracted its own clientele, and from around 1688 a coffeehouse kept by Edward Lloyd drew ship captains, shipowners, and merchants with an interest in overseas trade. That information made his premises a natural place to arrange marine insurance. Because they wrote under the description of the risk, these backers came to be called underwriters, a term still in use. Glance at three coins on a table and you know at once that there are three; nothing that feels like counting takes place. With nine coins the experience is different, and you must either count or estimate. In 1871 the economist William Stanley Jevons reported a simple test of this ability. He threw handfuls of beans toward a box and, glancing at those that landed inside, called out their number. He made no errors when three or four beans fell in, but his mistakes grew as the number increased.

In 1949 a team of psychologists named this rapid, accurate judgment of small quantities subitizing, from the Latin word for "sudden." Later laboratory studies, in which people report the number of dots flashed briefly on a screen, have found a consistent pattern. Response times rise only slightly from one item to four, then climb steeply with each additional item, and errors become common. The boundary varies somewhat from person to person but is usually placed at about four.

Why this limit exists is disputed. One proposal is that small sets form familiar patterns: two points make a line and three a triangle, so the number can be recognized much as a shape is. Another links subitizing to a limited capacity for keeping track of separate objects at the same time, a capacity that seems to hold only about four items. The two explanations are not necessarily exclusive, and some researchers suspect that both contribute.

When Dmitri Mendeleev published his periodic table in 1869, he arranged the known elements by atomic weight so that elements with similar properties fell into the same groups. Where the pattern seemed to require an element that no one had found, he left a gap rather than force a known element into the wrong place. In 1871 he went further and described several of the missing elements in detail, predicting their atomic weights, densities, and the compounds they would form. One he called eka-aluminium, meaning roughly "one place beyond aluminium."

In 1875 the French chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran detected a new element in a zinc ore by spotting unfamiliar lines in its spectrum, and he named it gallium. Its properties matched Mendeleev's eka-aluminium closely, with one apparent exception: the first measurement gave a density of about 4.7 grams per cubic centimeter, well below Mendeleev's figure of about 5.9. The discoveries of scandium in 1879 and germanium in 1886, both also fitting Mendeleev's descriptions, did much to persuade chemists that his table reflected something real. Around 1700, Bartolomeo Cristofori, a keyboard maker employed by Prince Ferdinando de' Medici in Florence, built an instrument that addressed a long-standing problem. The harpsichord, the leading keyboard instrument of the day, sounds by plucking its strings with small quills, and its volume changes very little however hard or gently a key is pressed. The clavichord, which strikes its strings with small metal blades, does respond to touch, but it is too quiet to be heard well in a large room.

Cristofori's solution was to strike the strings with leather-covered hammers. The difficulty lay in the mechanism. A hammer pressed against a string and held there would deaden the sound it had just produced, so the hammer had to strike and then fall back at once, even while the player's finger still held the key down. Cristofori's design included a device, now called an escapement, that released the hammer just before it reached the string, letting it rebound freely. Because the force of the blow now depended on the player's touch, the instrument could play both softly and loudly, and it came to be called the pianoforte, from the Italian words for "soft" and "loud."

The invention spread slowly. Only three of Cristofori's pianos survive, all from the 1720s. A detailed description published in 1711 by the writer Scipione Maffei was later translated into German, and the German organ builder Gottfried Silbermann went on to build pianos of his own, apparently drawing on Cristofori's design.
